pos: n. (the sixth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the heading of the sixth stanza of Psalm 119)
etymology: Hebrew waw, a hook or peg, the sixth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; rendered Vau by the Authorized Version in the headings of Psalm 119.
biblical_def: Vau is the sixth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and stands as the heading of the sixth stanza of Psalm 119, where the Authorized Version prints it in the text itself: “VAU. Let thy mercies come also unto me, O LORD, even thy salvation, according to thy word” (Psalm 119:41). The whole psalm is an acrostic of twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter, and every one of the eight verses in a stanza begins in Hebrew with that letter. The letter waw is a hook or peg, and in Hebrew grammar it is the joining letter, the and that couples clause to clause. The stanza it heads is a stanza of joining: mercy coupled to salvation, salvation coupled to the word, the word coupled to an answer for the mocker — “So shall I have wherewith to answer him that reproacheth me: for I trust in thy word” (Psalm 119:42). The psalmist then declares the liberty that comes of being bound to God's precepts: “And I will walk at liberty: for I seek thy precepts” (Psalm 119:45), and closes with delight: “And I will delight myself in thy commandments, which I have loved” (Psalm 119:47). That the Holy Ghost ordered a psalm by the letters of a language is no trifle. It teaches that God condescends to the forms of human speech, and that the plainest scaffolding of a tongue may be made to carry the praise of His law.

corruption_summary: The structure of Scripture is treated as decoration; the acrostic of Psalm 119 is part of the inspired text, not a flourish laid over it.
corruption_paragraphs: Readers trained to skim treat the letter headings as typographical ornament and pass over them. They are not ornament. The Holy Ghost shaped this psalm so that a man learning his letters would be learning the law of God at the same hour, and so that the memory would have handholds. To despise the form is to despise a kindness.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that inspiration reaches the shape of a text as well as its sense, and that God binds His people to Himself with the ordinary hooks of their own language.

pos: n. (the ninth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the heading of the ninth stanza of Psalm 119)
etymology: Hebrew teth, the ninth letter of the Hebrew alphabet, anciently a coil or a wheel; rendered Teth by the Authorized Version in Psalm 119.
biblical_def: Teth is the ninth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and heads the ninth stanza of Psalm 119: “TETH. Thou hast dealt well with thy servant, O LORD, according unto thy word” (Psalm 119:65). The eight verses under this letter are the psalm's great confession that affliction is good. The psalmist does not say that affliction is pleasant, nor that it is explicable; he says it was good for him: “Before I was afflicted I went astray: but now have I kept thy word” (Psalm 119:67). He traces the chastening to the hand of a good God, not a grudging one: “Thou art good, and doest good; teach me thy statutes” (Psalm 119:68). And he names the fruit of the rod in one line that has carried many saints through a dark providence: “It is good for me that I have been afflicted; that I might learn thy statutes” (Psalm 119:71). Every Hebrew verse of this stanza opens with teth, and the Hebrew word for good, tob, begins with that letter — so the letter itself preaches the stanza. The ninth letter is the letter of goodness, and under it stands the goodness of God in wounding His own.

corruption_summary: Affliction is treated as an interruption of the good life; under Teth it is named good, and the sufferer thanks God for it.
corruption_paragraphs: The common assumption is that a good God would keep a believing man from pain, so that pain must mean either God's absence or His displeasure. The ninth stanza of Psalm 119 denies both. The psalmist went astray while comfortable and kept the word once wounded, and he blesses God for the wound. The rod is not the opposite of the mercy; it is one of its instruments.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that chastening is fatherly, that God is good when He wounds as truly as when He heals, and that a saint may bless Him for the affliction itself.

pos: n. (the tenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the heading of the tenth stanza of Psalm 119)
etymology: Hebrew yod, a hand, the tenth and smallest letter of the Hebrew alphabet; rendered Jod by the Authorized Version in Psalm 119, and jot in the Gospel of Matthew.
biblical_def: Jod is the tenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet, the smallest character in the Hebrew script, and it heads the tenth stanza of Psalm 119: “JOD. Thy hands have made me and fashioned me: give me understanding, that I may learn thy commandments” (Psalm 119:73). The Hebrew name means a hand, and the stanza it heads begins with the hands of God forming the man who prays. Under this letter the psalmist owns that his very afflictions were measured out in faithfulness: “I know, O LORD, that thy judgments are right, and that thou in faithfulness hast afflicted me” (Psalm 119:75), and he asks for the one thing that makes a believer useful to other believers: “They that fear thee will be glad when they see me; because I have hoped in thy word” (Psalm 119:74). The stanza closes with a plea for inward soundness rather than outward reputation: “Let my heart be sound in thy statutes; that I be not ashamed” (Psalm 119:80). This letter has a further honor. Our Lord took the smallest letter of the alphabet as His measure of the law's permanence, and the Authorized Version renders it jot: not one stroke of it shall fail.

corruption_summary: Small things in Scripture are counted negligible; the smallest letter of the alphabet is the Lord's own measure of what cannot pass away.
corruption_paragraphs: Men who would not deny the Bible outright will still allow that a detail here or a stroke there may be given up without loss. Our Lord chose the smallest letter in the Hebrew alphabet to say the opposite. If the least character stands until all is fulfilled, then there is no stroke in Scripture a man may trade away, and no doctrine small enough to be surrendered for peace.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the entire trustworthiness of the written word down to its least letter, and the hands of God as the maker of the man who reads it.

pos: n. (the twelfth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the heading of the twelfth stanza of Psalm 119)
etymology: Hebrew lamed, an ox-goad, the twelfth letter of the Hebrew alphabet, kin to the verb lamad, to teach or to learn; rendered Lamed by the Authorized Version in Psalm 119. It is unrelated to the English adjective lame, which it merely resembles in spelling.
biblical_def: Lamed is the twelfth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and heads the twelfth stanza of Psalm 119, which opens with the shortest and steadiest line in the psalm: “LAMED. For ever, O LORD, thy word is settled in heaven” (Psalm 119:89). The letter's name is the ox-goad, the tool that teaches a beast its furrow, and it is kin to the Hebrew verb to teach. The stanza it heads is the psalm's doctrine of the unchangeableness of God's word and the stability of the creation that hangs upon it: “Thy faithfulness is unto all generations: thou hast established the earth, and it abideth” (Psalm 119:90), and “They continue this day according to thine ordinances: for all are thy servants” (Psalm 119:91). The sun, the sea and the seasons keep their appointments because a word holds them. Then the psalmist measures everything else against that word and finds it short: “I have seen an end of all perfection: but thy commandment is exceeding broad” (Psalm 119:96). Every human excellence has a boundary a man can walk to; the commandment of God has none. The goad teaches, and what it teaches here is that heaven settled the word before earth was laid.

corruption_summary: God's word is treated as a product of its age; under Lamed it is settled in heaven before the earth was established.
corruption_paragraphs: Every generation is told that the Scriptures are the voice of their own century and must be revised by ours. The twelfth stanza answers that the word was settled in heaven, not drafted on earth, and that the creation itself holds its course by that word. A rule that founded the world is not corrected by the world.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the eternity and immutability of God's word, and the exceeding breadth of a commandment that no human perfection reaches.

pos: n. (the thirteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the heading of the thirteenth stanza of Psalm 119)
etymology: Hebrew mem, water, the thirteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; rendered Mem by the Authorized Version in Psalm 119.
biblical_def: Mem is the thirteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and heads the thirteenth stanza of Psalm 119: “MEM. O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day” (Psalm 119:97). The name of the letter is water, and the stanza under it is all about a law taken in as a man takes in food and drink. It is the psalm's classic passage on meditation and on the plain profit of knowing Scripture better than one's adversaries do: “Thou through thy commandments hast made me wiser than mine enemies: for they are ever with me” (Psalm 119:98). The wisdom is not native shrewdness but a borrowed wisdom, and the borrowing is constant — the commandments are ever with me. Then comes the line that has sent generations of believers back to the text with an appetite: “How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!” (Psalm 119:103). Sweetness is not the end of it; understanding follows, and understanding sharpens into hatred of what is false: “Through thy precepts I get understanding: therefore I hate every false way” (Psalm 119:104). Love, meditation, taste, understanding, and then a settled hatred of error — that is the order the thirteenth stanza lays down.

corruption_paragraphs: Meditation now commonly means the emptying of the mind, a method borrowed from the religions of the east and sold as a health practice. The thirteenth stanza of Psalm 119 means the opposite: a mind full of a particular law, turned over all the day, tasted like honey, until it yields understanding. The one empties; the other fills.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the letter itself. The principle to recover is biblical meditation — a loving, continual occupation with the written word that makes a man wiser than his enemies and sets him against every false way.

pos: n. (the fifteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the heading of the fifteenth stanza of Psalm 119)
etymology: Hebrew samek, a prop or support, the fifteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; rendered Samech by the Authorized Version in Psalm 119.
biblical_def: Samech is the fifteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and heads the fifteenth stanza of Psalm 119: “SAMECH. I hate vain thoughts: but thy law do I love” (Psalm 119:113). The letter's name is a prop, the thing set under a weight to hold it up, and the stanza is about what a man leans on. Having set his hatred against empty thinking, the psalmist names his refuge: “Thou art my hiding place and my shield: I hope in thy word” (Psalm 119:114). The prop is not his resolve but God Himself, and the holding is God's work: “Uphold me according unto thy word, that I may live: and let me not be ashamed of my hope” (Psalm 119:116). A believer upheld by God does not therefore grow careless of God; the stanza ends in trembling: “My flesh trembleth for fear of thee; and I am afraid of thy judgments” (Psalm 119:120). Love and fear stand together here without apology. The man who hates vanity, loves the law, hides in God, is held up by God, and shakes before God's judgments is one man and not four, and the fifteenth letter names what carries him.

corruption_paragraphs: It is widely assumed that a God truly loved cannot be truly feared, and that trembling belongs to an immature faith. The fifteenth stanza of Psalm 119 puts love and dread in the same mouth without embarrassment. The man who says he hates vain thoughts and loves the law is the same man whose flesh trembles for fear of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God Himself is the prop under a believer's life, that he is upheld by promise and not by resolve, and that filial fear is part of love, not its enemy.

pos: n. (the nineteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the heading of the nineteenth stanza of Psalm 119)
etymology: Hebrew qoph, anciently the back of the head or the eye of a needle, the nineteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; rendered Koph by the Authorized Version in Psalm 119.
biblical_def: Koph is the nineteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and heads the nineteenth stanza of Psalm 119, the stanza of early and whole-hearted prayer: “KOPH. I cried with my whole heart; hear me, O LORD: I will keep thy statutes” (Psalm 119:145). Hebrew qara, to call or to cry, begins with this letter, and the stanza is built on crying. The prayer is not a divided prayer, and it is not a prayer that leaves obedience for later; the man who cries with his whole heart promises in the same breath to keep the statutes. He asks for rescue with his eye on the testimonies: “I cried unto thee; save me, and I shall keep thy testimonies” (Psalm 119:146). Then comes one of the great lines on rising early to pray: “I prevented the dawning of the morning, and cried: I hoped in thy word” (Psalm 119:147) — he was awake before the light was. And the stanza grounds all this crying on something older than the crier: “Concerning thy testimonies, I have known of old that thou hast founded them for ever” (Psalm 119:152). Prayer that reaches heaven leans on a word that was founded before the one praying was born.

pos: n. (the twentieth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the heading of the twentieth stanza of Psalm 119)
etymology: Hebrew resh, a head, the twentieth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; rendered Resh by the Authorized Version in Psalm 119.
biblical_def: Resh is the twentieth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and heads the twentieth stanza of Psalm 119, which is a plea out of trouble: “RESH. Consider mine affliction, and deliver me: for I do not forget thy law” (Psalm 119:153). The letter's name is a head, and the Hebrew verb raah, to see or to look upon, begins with it — which is the burden of the stanza. The psalmist asks God to look, to take his case in hand as an advocate takes a brief: “Plead my cause, and deliver me: quicken me according to thy word” (Psalm 119:154). He appeals not to his innocence but to his love: “Consider how I love thy precepts: quicken me, O LORD, according to thy lovingkindness” (Psalm 119:159). Twice he asks to be quickened, which is to be made alive, and both times the measure is outside himself — once God's word, once God's lovingkindness. The stanza closes on the ground of the whole psalm: “Thy word is true from the beginning: and every one of thy righteous judgments endureth for ever” (Psalm 119:160). The afflicted man is not asking God to invent a mercy; he is asking Him to act on a word already true from the beginning.

corruption_paragraphs: A word that is true only when it works for the hearer is no word at all, and that is the account of Scripture now commonly offered: a text that becomes true in the encounter. The twentieth stanza says God's word is true from the beginning — before the reader, outside the reader, and whether or not the reader is delivered yet.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an afflicted saint pleads a word already true, asks God to plead his cause, and seeks life by measure of divine lovingkindness rather than personal desert.

pos: n. (the twenty-first letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the heading of the twenty-first stanza of Psalm 119)
etymology: Hebrew shin, a tooth, the twenty-first letter of the Hebrew alphabet; rendered Schin by the Authorized Version in Psalm 119.
biblical_def: Schin is the twenty-first letter of the Hebrew alphabet and heads the twenty-first stanza of Psalm 119, the stanza of a persecuted man who is nevertheless at peace: “SCHIN. Princes have persecuted me without a cause: but my heart standeth in awe of thy word” (Psalm 119:161). The great men of the earth are against him and he is not afraid of them; his dread is reserved for God's word. What follows is joy out of all proportion to his circumstances: “I rejoice at thy word, as one that findeth great spoil” (Psalm 119:162) — the gladness of a soldier stumbling on a treasure, not the mild satisfaction of a reader. Then the promise that has quieted countless troubled saints: “Great peace have they which love thy law: and nothing shall offend them” (Psalm 119:165). Peace is not promised to the undisturbed but to those who love the law, and the word rendered offend means to stumble; they have no stumblingblock. The stanza ends in the open: “I have kept thy precepts and thy testimonies: for all my ways are before thee” (Psalm 119:168). He obeys as a man watched, and the watching is his comfort rather than his terror.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the fear of God's word displaces the fear of men, that Scripture is found like great spoil, and that those who love the law have nothing to stumble over.

etymology: Hebrew tav, a mark or sign, the twenty-second and last letter of the Hebrew alphabet; rendered Tau by the Authorized Version in Psalm 119.
biblical_def: Tau is the twenty-second and last letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and it heads the final stanza of Psalm 119: “TAU. Let my cry come near before thee, O LORD: give me understanding according to thy word” (Psalm 119:169). The name of the letter is a mark or sign — the character set upon a thing to show whose it is. After a hundred and sixty-eight verses in praise of the law, the psalm does not end in mastery. It ends in asking: “Let my supplication come before thee: deliver me according to thy word” (Psalm 119:170), and in longing: “I have longed for thy salvation, O LORD; and thy law is my delight” (Psalm 119:174). And then the last verse of the longest psalm in Scripture is a confession of straying and a plea to be fetched home: “I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek thy servant; for I do not forget thy commandments” (Psalm 119:176). The man who has celebrated the law from aleph to tau closes by calling himself a lost sheep and asking the Shepherd to come after him. That is the whole doctrine of the psalm in one line: the law is perfect, the lover of the law is not, and the seeking is God's to do.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Tau is the name of a Hebrew letter and has no entry in Webster's dictionary of the English language.
webster_full: Tau is the name of the twenty-second and last letter of the Hebrew alphabet; Webster's 1828 dictionary treats common English words and does not define it.
The Authorized Version prints it as the heading of Psalm 119:169.
The Hebrew name denotes a mark or a sign.
Its stanza closes the longest psalm in Scripture.
The stanza runs from Psalm 119:169 to Psalm 119:176.

corruption_summary: Bible knowledge is mistaken for spiritual arrival; under Tau the psalm ends with a lost sheep asking to be sought.
corruption_paragraphs: A man who knows the Scriptures well is tempted to think himself safe by knowing them, and others are tempted to think so of him. The last stanza of Psalm 119 forbids it. The psalmist, having gone through the whole alphabet in praise of the law, ends by naming himself a straying sheep and asking God to seek him out.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the knowledge of Scripture ends in dependence, not in self-sufficiency, and that the seeking of a straying servant is the Shepherd's work.
